section_1.content: Briefly define a basis as a set of 'coordinate axes' (vectors). A vector is just an arrow; its coordinates change based on the grid we draw behind it.
section_1.example: Visual: A single arrow on a 2D plane. Show how it can be described by standard axes (x=1, y=2) versus a tilted, skewed grid.

section_2.title: The Problem: Changing Perspectives
section_2.content: Introduce the need to represent the same vector 'v' in two different bases, B and C. Explain that we need a bridge to translate coordinates from one system to another.
section_2.example: Character: A drone flying in a room. The drone measures its position relative to the wall (Basis B), but the pilot measures it relative to their own position (Basis C).

section_3.title: The Transition Matrix (The Bridge)
section_3.content: Define the transition matrix P as the matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the new basis vectors expressed in the old basis. Formula: [v]_B = P * [v]_C.
section_3.example: Animation: Show the basis vectors of C being 'decomposed' into the components of B. This mapping creates the columns of matrix P.

section_4.title: Step-by-Step Calculation
section_4.content: Demonstrate the algorithm: 1. Identify basis vectors, 2. Form matrix P, 3. Multiply P by new coordinates to recover old coordinates.
section_4.example: Math: Let B = { (1,0), (0,1) } and C = { (1,1), (-1,1) }. Transition matrix P = [[1, -1], [1, 1]]. Transform point [1, 0]_C to [1, 1]_B.

section_5.title: Real-World Application & Summary
section_5.content: Conclude by showing why we do this: simplifying complex linear transformations (e.g., rotation/scaling) by choosing a 'friendlier' basis.
section_5.example: Device: A game engine changing from 'World Space' (fixed map) to 'Camera Space' (what the player sees) to render 3D graphics efficiently.
